alignments.note: Ordinary conditional particle aligned to the English *if* that introduces the protasis; rule 72's closing clause treats an ordinary conditional like any other word.
Postpositive connective realized by the verse-initial *Now*; rule 15 permits the reordering.

The article governing ἵππων takes the English *the* of *the horses' bridles* (rule 19). Competing reading: give *the* to s005 as the determiner of *bridles* and leave s003 unrepresented; taken this way because the ASV writes *the* immediately before the word answering to ἵππων, and the possessive *horses'* is what displaces the determiner of *bridles* under rule 20, exactly as `ὁ θρόνος τοῦ Σατανᾶ` → *Satan's throne* does.
Genitive noun rendered by the English possessive *horses'* (token supplied without its apostrophe).

The genitive ἵππων already occupies the determiner slot of *bridles* as an English *'s* possessive, so this article realizes nothing (rule 20, which names a genitive noun the ASV renders with *'s* as one of the words that can displace it).
Noun to noun.

Preposition governing the prepositional phrase realizes the Greek preposition (rule 36). Variant SBLGNT.JAS.3.3.v002 is underdetermined between the base εἰς and r01; the fallback remains among the readings the English permits, so rule 97 is not in question.

The article is what the supplied possessive *their* realizes (rule 20, second arm). No genitive pronoun stands with `στόματα`, and rule 76's availability test settles the three candidates that do stand in the verse: `ἵππων` is already spent on *horses'*, `αὐτούς` on the subject *they*, and `αὐτῶν` — the strongest challenger, a genitive pronoun of the same person and number — on the *their* of *their body*. None is available to carry this possessive. The corpus decides this configuration the same way and often: JHN.2.12 has two `αὐτοῦ`, each spent on its own phrase, and gives the middle article a supplied *his*; 1PE.2.12 `ἐκ τῶν καλῶν ἔργων` → *by your good works* aligns the article with two `ὑμῶν` standing; and 2PE.1.5 writes both treatments in one verse, as this verse does. The competing reading is rule 23 `unrepresented`, refused because the ASV writes a determiner here; the corpus reserves that for a shared genitive scoping over coordinated nouns (REV.1.14, EPH.2.1), which is not this construction.
Noun to noun.
Finite verb with its inflection-licensed subject pronoun; head on the lexical verb rather than the subject (rules 9, 17).

Preposition governing the articular infinitive takes the whole English clause-introducer (rule 61); here that is the bare complementizer *that*, which rule 24 treats as one analysis with *to the end that*.
Nominalizing article of the articular infinitive; English spells no word answering to the article itself (rule 61).
Infinitive expanded into a finite clause; the modal *may* is its helper and the head is the lexical verb (rules 7, 9, 17).
Expressed accusative subject of the infinitive, rendered by the English subject pronoun *they*. Rule 74 does not bear on this: it governs a subject Greek leaves unexpressed, and this one is written.
Dative complement to the English object pronoun.

Adverbial καί realized by the clause-final *also*, aligned on rule 65's English-side test; rule 15 permits the discontinuity from its Greek position. No οὕτως stands here, so rule 100 is not in question.
Attributive adjective to *whole*.
The free genitive pronoun αὐτῶν occupies the determiner slot as *their*, so this article realizes nothing (rule 20 proper).
Noun to noun.
Genitive pronoun rendered by the possessive *their* (rule 20).

Finite verb with its subject pronoun; *about* is the English phrasal verb's own particle and governs no prepositional phrase, so rule 36's contrast keeps it inside the unit. Head on *turn*, the word that glosses μετάγω, rather than on the particle or the subject (rules 17, 91): *turn* is no empty support verb, so rule 91's `make straight` case does not reach it.

review_notes: Accepted alignment is confirmed unchanged in unit membership and heads; only three notes were sharpened (see below). Every s001-s021 and t001-t022 id is partitioned exactly once.

s003/s005 is the one materially contestable pair. τῶν ἵππων τοὺς χαλινούς → *the horses' bridles*: the English *the* is the determiner of *horses'*, so it goes to τῶν, and τούς is emptied by the *'s* possessive under rule 20's genitive-noun clause. The competing reading (bare *the* on τούς, τῶν unrepresented) is named in the s003 note.

s008 note now cites rule 76 by name. Both candidate possessors present in the verse are already spent — ἵππων on *horses'*, αὐτούς on *they* — so availability, not mere presence, is what leaves the article to carry *their*. This is the contrast with s018, where αὐτῶν is free and rule 20 proper empties the article; the verse writes both configurations, as JHN's rule 76 example does.
s001's note previously cited rule 40, which governs a subordinator realized by an infinitival *to*; replaced with the ordinary-conditional reading. No alignment consequence.

s021 keeps *about* inside the verb's unit: μετάγω is rendered by the phrasal *turn about* with *their whole body* as its object, and no Greek preposition stands for *about* to answer to under rule 36. Head on *turn* per rule 91's operational test — the corpus spends the verb word on μετάγω (cf. μετάγεται in the next verse), and *about* is the particle, not a meaning-bearing complement.

Variant note for the chapter log: SBLGNT.JAS.3.3.v002 is underdetermined and its fallback is still among the readings the English permits, so it carries no FALLBACK EXCLUDED mark and rule 97 does not apply; v001 is compatible with the base. No textual decision is made inside this file (rule 12).
